articles.headline: How to restore dignity to the world of work | Letters
articles.teaser: Colin Montgomery suggests that expectations should be properly managed. Plus letters from Paul Hartley, Hartley Dean and Peter ThorntonJohn Harris’s jeremiad about what the world of work has become (A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue, 22 November) put me in mind of the old joke: “How do I get to Dublin?” “Well, I wouldn’t start from here.” Because, as he concludes, there’s almost no chance of any government being able to even begin to relieve this situation quickly, short of putting an emergency brake on 40 years of neoliberalism. As if.I’d like to suggest a real starting point for the fightback against this seemingly interminable malaise that looks set to blight generations to come: namely, begin from somewhere grounded in properly managed expectations. It is therefore not surprising that major psychological distress can lead to physical symptoms, and the other way around.However, as a GP, I would recommend being extremely careful about equating “otherwise unexplained symptoms” with psychosomatic illness. articles.headline: The most surprising thing about Burnham’s slow politics is this: it could be working | Andy Beckett
articles.teaser: ‘Andy time’ may frustrate the media and voters impatient for change – but after years of short premierships and rushed policies, isn’t this the reset Westminster needs?Andy Burnham is making a lot of people impatient. Political journalists, pro-EU activists, climate campaigners, fossil-fuel lobbyists, recipients of welfare benefits, advocates of welfare cuts, enemies of neoliberalism, enthusiasts for renationalisation, members of the armed forces and even cabinet colleagues: all are waiting for the prime minister to make big decisions, and thus reveal the true nature of his administration, four months after its beginning.Since his Manchester mayoralty, some of Burnham’s co-workers have had a phrase for his tendency to take things at his own tempo: “Andy time”. He lets interesting conversations overrun, likes to ponder issues without being rushed, and pushes back crucial announcements. The unveiling of his 10-year plan – a typically ambitious but loose Burnham timespan, and one of his government’s pivotal moments – has been repeatedly delayed.

articles.headline: The Guardian view on fostering: ceremonies and sibling rights should help care leavers | Editorial
articles.teaser: Ministers have recognised that young adults need more support. But children’s social care reform must go deeperThe first lifelong guardianship ceremonies, held in Northampton last week with Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, among the guests, are the latest in a series of measures aimed at boosting support for care leavers. While the decision to register a link between a person who has been looked after as a child and another adult such as a former carer or friend does not carry legal obligations, those involved spoke movingly about what it meant for these relationships to be formally recognised. New rules requiring councils to support contact between siblings in the care system are similarly aimed at strengthening networks that could sustain them beyond childhood into adult life.Belatedly, the government is acting on a mound of evidence that children who are taken into local authority care are frequently acutely vulnerable when they come out of it as 18-year-olds.

Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan.

articles.headline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.teaser: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam.Aditya’s suggested reading:To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair.For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books.To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian.Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak.Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch.Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory PartyFor more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers.
